newsitem.title: USA: Chubb chief warns on insurance changes.
newsitem.headline: Chubb chief warns on insurance changes.

text.p: U.S. insurers must focus on what they are good at in order to cope with dramatic changes sweeping through the industry, Chubb Group Chairman and Chief Executive Dean O'Hare said on Thursday.

Continued mergers, downsizing, excess capacity, and competition from nontraditional players will force insurers to become more specialized in the future, O'Hare told participants at an insurance conference.
"The mistake we all make too often in our industry is to try to be all things to all people," O'Hare said.
"The desire to serve every need of every customer is natural, but misguided and unachievable."
This is why the New Jersey-based Chubb decided to get out of the life insurance business earlier this year, O'Hare said.

He said that in the life sector, "It is increasingly clear that the future winners in this business will be the giant companies whose economies of scale and distribution give them a virtually unbeatable advantage over smaller competition."
O'Hare said he took little comfort from the recent industry trend of strong profits.
"Too much capacity is chasing too little business in the domestic U.S. market. We are now entering our tenth straight year of intense price competition."
"Sooner or later, we're going to have to pay the piper. But so long as catastrophes are kind to us, reinsurance is readily available... we will be faced with a weakened market."

He said the surplus of capacity hurts not only insurers but their clients, "since low prices and unprofitable underwriting tempt some companies to make up the difference with high-risk investments and elastic reserve structures, especially with respect to long-term environmental risks."
O'Hare said the advent of the Internet is the great "wild card" of the industry's future.
"It is still too early to assess its impact. We are already seeing commodity products, such as term life and auto policies, sold over the net."
"The revolution is unlikely to stop there. It could potentially impact all areas of our business."
"In the face of all this market change, insurance companies must focus our energy and resources on what we're good at, who are customers are, and what our customers need."
